# UMA for Agents

> Decentralized agent authorization built on User-Managed Access (UMA 2.0). The resource owner sets her terms once, and other people's AI agents negotiate against them while she is offline. A working proof-of-concept, with a lab you can run.

A working proof-of-concept, with Eve Maler, carrying User-Managed Access
(UMA) 2.0 into the agent era: the resource owner sets policy once, and other
people's AI agents negotiate access against it while she is offline. The lab
runs locally with one command and also deploys to Kubernetes.

Every page below is available as plain Markdown by appending `.md` to its
URL. The site also speaks MCP at https://u4a.ai/mcp with four tools —
`listDocs`, `getDoc`, `listBlogs` and `getBlog` — if you would rather read
it that way.

## Documentation

Concept pages explain one idea; guides walk a procedure end to end; the
reference is the wire contract, the endpoints and the deviations from
UMA 2.0. Listed in reading order.

- [Overview · Overview](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview.md): A working profile of UMA 2.0 for the case where the thing asking is someone else's AI agent, and the person who owns the resource is asleep.
- [Overview · Why the owner decides](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/why.md): What breaks when the party who owns a resource is not the party who configured access to it.
- [Overview · Architecture](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/architecture.md): Which party holds which responsibility, and why the boundaries between them are the design.
- [Overview · Concepts](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/concepts.md): Every idea the rest of the documentation assumes, each in a paragraph, in the order the pieces meet each other.
- [Overview · Standards this composes](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/standards.md): Every specification U4A builds on, what each one supplies, and where it appears in the flow.
- [Overview · The four beats](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/four-beats.md): Challenge, attempt, commit, grant — the whole negotiation, and what each exchange is for.
- [Overview · The three parties](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/parties.md): Owner, requesting party, requesting agent — and what it costs to treat the last two as one.
- [Overview · Terms as first-class](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/terms.md): The owner does not just decide — she states what she requires, and the agent signs it.
- [Overview · The two intents](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/two-intents.md): Who decides whether an AI agent is doing what it said it would — the agent's operator, or the owner of the data it is touching. How U4A answers that, and what the owner can check for herself.
- [Overview · Her own agent](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/first-party.md): The case where the person asking and the person who owns the data are the same. Why it needs the same protocol anyway, and what changes when she activated the agent herself.
- [Overview · Identity is not authorization](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/identity.md): Knowing which agent is calling tells you nothing about whether it may proceed. Both are needed, and they answer different questions.
- [Overview · Identity stays where it is](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/flow.md): The owner never has to know how the asking agent is identified — checked against four identity regimes that produce one unchanged decision.
- [Overview · Discovery, public and protected](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/discovery.md): What a resource is can be public. Whose instances sit behind it cannot.
- [Overview · Proof-of-possession](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/proof-of-possession.md): A grant that names a key, and a request signed with it — so holding the token is not enough.
- [Overview · Single-use means indivisible](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/single-use.md): Once has to mean once across every replica, which makes it a property of how you write to the store rather than of the protocol.
- [Overview · Revocation and the ledger](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/revocation.md): What was promised, what was approved, what was touched — and what happens the moment the owner changes her mind.
- [Overview · Agent assurance](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/assurance.md): What the owner's own authority can verify about an agent asking for her things — and why nothing an agent says about itself can widen access.
- [Overview · The owner's attention](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/attention.md): The scarcest resource in an owner-decides design, why an unbounded pending queue is a denial-of-service surface, and how to cap it without shutting out the agent you wanted.
- [Overview · Many owners, one resource server](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/multi-owner.md): A firm holds many people's accounts, and each of them may name a different authorization server — including one the firm was never configured against.
- [Overview · Shared ownership](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/shared-ownership.md): A firm owns a book, shares parts of it with the people who work on it, and sets policy over it that none of them can waive — while each of them still administers access under her own authority.
- [Overview · Joint ownership](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/joint-ownership.md): Two people hold an account together and neither can release it alone. What counts the votes owns nothing, decides nothing, and does not have to be trusted.
- [Overview · Compared to UMA 2.0](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/compare-uma.md): What this profile keeps, what it changes, and why each change was necessary rather than preferred.
- [Overview · Compared to OAuth 2.0 and GNAP](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/compare-oauth-gnap.md): OAuth, CIBA-style asynchronous authorization and GNAP can all carry a negotiation. None of them, on its own, puts the deciding party anywhere but the service.
- [Overview · Compared to policy engines](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/compare-policy-engines.md): OPA, Cedar and AuthZEN decide well. They do not decide whose policy is being expressed, and the two compose.
- [Overview · Compared to agent identity work](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/compare-agent-identity.md): AAuth, Web Bot Auth, CIMD and enterprise-managed agent auth — what each answers, and what is left over.
- [Overview · Glossary](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/glossary.md): Terms as this documentation uses them, including the places where a word means something narrower here than it does elsewhere.
- [Overview · FAQ](https://u4a.ai/docs/overview/faq.md): The questions that come up first, answered directly, including the ones where the answer is that this does not do that.
- [Guides · The roles you must fill](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/roles.md): Six roles, what each one has to be able to do, and how to judge whether something in your stack can do it.
- [Guides · Run the lab](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/run-the-lab.md): A three-node deployment with one command, then the sequence that shows an owner deciding while she is the only one who can.
- [Guides · Choose an enforcement point](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/enforcement-point.md): What the component that refuses has to be able to do, the two shapes it can take, and how to keep one implementation behind both.
- [Guides · Issue the challenge](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/challenge.md): Turning a refusal into the start of a negotiation — what the challenge carries, and the check that stops it being redirected.
- [Guides · Dictate terms, take an agreement](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/terms.md): How the owner's side proffers the conditions of access, what a signed echo has to prove, and the checks that stop an agent agreeing to something weaker.
- [Guides · Mint an operation-bound grant](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/grant.md): Issuing a credential that authorizes one operation rather than a capability, and the enforcement order that makes it hold.
- [Guides · Make single-use indivisible](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/indivisible.md): Why the burn has to be one statement, how to write it in a relational store, and how to test something that only fails under concurrency.
- [Guides · Wire the owner's approval path](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/approval.md): Holding a negotiation while a human decides, showing her something she can act on, and authorizing her without inventing a credential for her.
- [Guides · Let the owner write her own policy](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/owner-policy.md): Terms she adds herself, rules about the requests that reach her, and the one validation that has to happen where policy is stored rather than where it is evaluated.
- [Guides · Put the authority on her device](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/personal-authority.md): Running the owner's side inside a personal AI — the credential it needs, the four methods it has to provide, and what stays the authorization server's job.
- [Guides · Deploy it at scale](https://u4a.ai/docs/guides/at-scale.md): Separating the parties so the seam is enforced rather than described, replicating an authority correctly, and the checks that prove it held.
- [Reference · Wire contract](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/wire-contract.md): Every message that travels between the parties, in order, with the fields that carry meaning.
- [Reference · Endpoints](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/endpoints.md): Every surface each party exposes, who may call it, and what it answers.
- [Reference · Events](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/events.md): The structured event stream, every event name, and the ledger projected from it.
- [Reference · MCP binding](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/mcp-binding.md): How the grant travels over Model Context Protocol — discovery channels, both challenge encodings, the pend, and what MCP's types cannot yet express.
- [Reference · Configuration](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/configuration.md): Every setting each component reads, its default, and the two settings people get wrong.
- [Reference · Deviations from UMA 2.0](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/deviations.md): The extension register — every place this profile departs from stock UMA, what the baseline says, and why each departure exists.
- [Reference · Findings](https://u4a.ai/docs/reference/findings.md): What the build produced for the people writing the specifications — verdicts on each UMA 2.0 primitive, twenty-five recommendations, and what was parked.

## Changelog

Every release, newest first. One entry per merged change; several land on
most days.

- [August 25 2026 · v2026.08.23](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Docs: a changelog at `/changelog/`, back to the first release. In `⌘K` search as one row per release, in `llms.txt`, in the sitemap, published as `/changelog.md`, and readable over MCP with a new `listChangelog` tool.
- [August 25 2026 · v2026.08.22](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Organization: a charter may only claim a namespace it names. `northwind-vault/*` is accepted; `*/get_positions` is refused.
- [August 25 2026 · v2026.08.21](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Joint ownership: a resource can have several owners of equal standing, none of whom can decide alone. A published mandate names who is entitled to be counted, at what weight and how many it takes; each owner's authority signs a verdict bound to one negotiation and one agreement; a tally collects them.
- [August 25 2026 · v2026.08.20](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Organization: an organization can own resources, share them with members under a role, and set policy over them. Each member administers access through her own authorization server and her own terms. New `org-authority` service.
- [August 23 2026 · v2026.08.19](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Authorization server: one resource server can hold many people's accounts, each governed by an authorization server of her own. Every owner-scoped artifact carries its owner: the ticket, the grant, the resource id, the terms template and the RFC 9728 document.
- [August 21 2026 · v2026.08.18](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): kagent: `make kagent-ask Q=…` asks your own question instead of a hardcoded one, and `SIM=0` lets a person answer the request rather than the check answering it.
- [August 21 2026 · v2026.08.17](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Licensing: `NOTICE` rewritten from a component-by-component audit, separating the application stack, the Kubernetes platform, the website and upstream checkouts. One licence had been stated incorrectly.
- [August 20 2026 · v2026.08.16](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Authorization server: `standing.first_party` — an agent is first-party when the operator it names is an origin the owner claimed *and* her authority found that agent's key published in that operator's directory.
- [August 19 2026 · v2026.08.15](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Authorization server: the derived `enforced` annotation was written through `publish_terms`, which is idempotent per template id — so on any store that had already published a version the field was dropped and never appeared. Postgres failed where the in-memory store passed, because the latter republishes on every boot.
- [August 19 2026 · v2026.08.14](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Authorization server: her terms mark which prohibitions the enforcement point refuses outright — `operation_mismatch` and `already_consumed` — rather than presenting every line as equally a matter of trust.
- [August 19 2026 · v2026.08.13](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Protocol: two optional requester-authored claims on the agreement — a stated reason and a cited mandate — recorded and shown to the owner, never judged. The requesting side previously had nowhere to say what it was asking for.
- [August 17 2026 · v2026.08.12](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): Docs: the assurance material split by subject — what an authority can verify, the owner's attention as a denial-of-service surface, revoking an operator rather than an agent, and a guide to writing rules.
- [The full changelog](https://u4a.ai/changelog.md): every release since the first.

## Posts

- [Everything You Need to Know About Deploying U4A at Scale](https://u4a.ai/blog/2026-08-12-deploying-u4a-at-scale.md): A field guide to running owner-authoritative authorization for real: how it differs from the policy engine you already run, the parts list, the five things that will bite you, a complete Kubernetes reference architecture on the solo.io stack — and an honest list of what it does not solve yet.
- [Let Them: A Developer's Guide to UMA for Agents](https://u4a.ai/blog/2026-08-06-let-them-a-developers-guide-to-u4a.md): The industry is fighting over how agents prove who they are. That is the wrong fight. The question that decides whether an agent economy works is whether the owner of a resource can set the terms — and U4A is what that looks like in running code.

## Source
